newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Mixed feelings greet Nigeria second bourse plan.
newsitem.headline: Mixed feelings greet Nigeria second bourse plan.

text.p: Operators on the Lagos floor of the Nigerian stock exchange on Wednesday expressed mixed feelings towards government plans for a second stock exchange in the federal capital Abuja in central Nigeria.
Finance minister Anthony Ani, who announced the plans on Tuesday, said the aim was to break the monopoly of the existing market based in the commercial hub of Lagos in the southwest.
Many traders said the move was not unexpected going by Ani's previous pronouncements but questioned the wisdom behind it.
"The proposal is ill-timed, ill-conceived and unreasonable," said Alex Osunde of Enterprise Stockbrokers. "People should not let their personal interest override national interest."
But Umar Faruk, a major investor in Nigerian equities, said a second exchange would help expand capital market activities throughout the country.
"If government is to privatise big parastatals, there is need to have another exchange that can accommodate the huge volume of shares," Faruk said.
He said the existing market was also not able to regulate its operations, making calls for a rival exchange realistic.
"Besides, another exchange in Abuja will enable investors in Northern Nigeria to trade their shares as people in Lagos are already doing," Faruk added.
The existing stock market was set up by private investors as the Lagos Stock Exchange in 1961 and later renamed the Nigerian Stock Exchange.
It has branches in Ibadan, Onitsha, Port Harcourt, Kaduna, Kano but the bulk of trading is done on the Lagos floor. Last year, its officials said an Abuja branch was in the pipeline.

They say the exchange with market capitalisation of more than 367 billion naira ($4.4 billion) could play a key role in attracting more foreign and domestic capital, but the government has blamed them for not doing enough to attract more funds.
However exchange operators counter that not much could be done unless government pursues a privatisation programme that would give it depth.
Ani set up a panel last year to investigate the exchange and its regulator, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
The panel, headed by merchant banker Dennis Odife, has since submitted its report and one newspaper said its recommendations included breaking the monopoly of the existing market.
